headline: Medium risk: shared-file PDF ingestion can enable prompt injection and data leakage; no direct evidence of tighter isolation between Argo Workflows and pdf.js.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Argo Workflows can pass artifacts through REST/gRPC and pdf.js reads PDF files in browser-based tests, so a shared file or artifact path could carry attacker-controlled content into a parser. The pair lacks documented provenance tracking or isolation, so injection is plausible even though no direct bridge is evidenced.
conditions: IF Argo outputs a PDF artifact that pdf.js later opens from a shared workspace
IF the PDF content is attacker-controlled and treated as instructions by downstream automation
mitigations: Store untrusted PDFs in a separate directory from workflow artifacts
Disable automatic handoff from Argo outputs to pdf.js inputs
Add a manual review step before opening generated PDFs
Use content provenance labels on every artifact
requires-engineering: enforce sandboxed, read-only ingestion for pdf.js

B_data_leakage.rationale: Argo Workflows touches artifacts and parameters and has allowlisted network egress, while pdf.js processes PDF documents from files. If sensitive data is embedded in PDFs or workflow artifacts, the pair can move it across components without a documented isolation boundary; the evidence is indirect, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF workflow artifacts contain sensitive parameters or embedded data
IF pdf.js is given PDFs from the same workspace as Argo outputs
mitigations: Separate sensitive and non-sensitive workspaces
Strip secrets from workflow parameters before artifact creation
Restrict which PDFs can be opened by pdf.js
Review network egress allowlist for artifact handlers
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning before artifact export

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Argo Workflows exposes API-based orchestration and pdf.js supports multiple instances, but the profiles do not show overlapping write targets, shared mutable state, or git/database access. A conflict is possible only if an external orchestrator maps both onto the same writable resource, so the blast radius is limited and configuration-dependent.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write to the same shared directory or artifact store
IF an external orchestrator omits locking around shared mutable resources
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Enable locking in the orchestrator
Run one agent at a time for shared resources
Audit for overlapping write paths
requires-engineering: add resource-level mutexes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Argo can generate workflow artifacts and pdf.js can render or inspect PDFs, so a downstream pipeline could treat Argo-produced content as authoritative input to pdf.js without verification. The profiles do not prove automatic action-taking, but the handoff pathway exists and could propagate bad facts or malformed documents.
conditions: IF pdf.js consumes PDFs generated by Argo without a validation step
IF downstream automation acts on rendered or extracted PDF content
mitigations: Insert checksum validation before pdf.js ingestion
Require human approval for generated PDFs
Compare extracted text against source metadata
Log provenance for each handoff
requires-engineering: add schema validation for workflow outputs

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and show no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch. Argo touches artifacts/parameters and pdf.js touches PDF documents, but the evidence does not show regulated data classes or conflicting compliance obligations, so only a low, documentation-gap risk remains.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is introduced into either workflow
IF an operator relies on undocumented retention or residency behavior
mitigations: Document data-class handling for both tools
Avoid regulated data in shared workflows
Set retention rules for generated PDFs
Review deployment region and storage location
requires-engineering: map compliance controls to each data flow
